sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to Interactive Lab 1! Scroll down directly below this slide to explore our Event-Time Watermarking and Sliding Window Studio. Experiment with out-of-order event streams, lateness thresholds, and window materializations.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Welcome to Interactive Lab 1! Dr. Nova and Kaito invite you to test watermark progression and window state buffers. Watch how tightening lateness tolerance drops stragglers to the Dead-Letter Queue.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 1! A streaming pipeline calculates watermarks as Current Max Event Time minus 10 seconds. An event arrives with timestamp 12:00:15 when the current watermark is 12:00:20. How does the stream engine handle it? Select Option A, Option B, or Option C.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Checkpoint 1, Kaito! Notice that timestamp 15 is strictly less than watermark 20. Which option correctly describes the stream engine's handling policy?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Masterclass comprehension! Because event timestamp 12:00:15 is strictly earlier than watermark 12:00:20, the event is classified as Late Data! Any windows ending at or before 12:00:15 have already materialized and emitted, so the record is dropped or routed to the Dead-Letter Queue side output.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Careful! A watermark is a monotonic completeness barrier. Once watermark W reaches 12:00:20, the engine assumes all prior events have been ingested and closes corresponding windows. A record with timestamp 12:00:15 is strictly late and cannot re-open finalized windows without allowed lateness.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to Interactive Lab 2! Scroll down directly below this slide to inspect our Streaming Backpressure and Kafka Partition Sizing Studio. Simulate Little's Law queue growth, observe buffer fill times, and balance partition workloads.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Welcome to Interactive Lab 2! Stress-test consumer worker queues under sudden arrival spikes. Watch the queue gauge hit red when arrival rate exceeds processing capacity, and scale partition counts to absorb massive throughput.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 2! A real-time surveillance pipeline computes 1-hour moving averages every 5 minutes. Applying our window state replication formula, into how many concurrent window buckets does each transaction event replicate? Select Option A, Option B, or Option C.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Checkpoint 2, Kaito! Window duration is 60 minutes and slide step is 5 minutes. Apply the ceiling formula to find the exact state replication multiplier.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Outstanding mathematical derivation! Window duration 60 minutes divided by slide step 5 minutes yields a state replication factor of exactly 12! Each transaction resides in 12 concurrent window accumulators in memory, multiplying state footprint by twelvefold over a tumbling window.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Not quite! The state replication factor R state equals the ceiling of window size divided by slide increment. Sixty minutes divided by five minutes is 12 active window state buckets, not a simple subtraction or single bucket.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 3! An ingestion spike delivers 15,000 messages per second against 9,000 consumer capacity with a 30,000 message buffer. Meanwhile, target throughput is 800 megabytes per second with a 50 megabytes per partition limit. Determine the buffer fill time and minimum partition count.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Checkpoint 3! Net queue growth is 6,000 messages per second into a 30,000 message buffer. And 800 megabytes divided by 50 megabytes gives the partition lower bound. Select Option A, Option B, or Option C.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Flawless systems architecture! Net queue growth of 6,000 messages per second exhausts the 30,000 buffer in exactly 5.00 seconds, triggering backpressure! And dividing 800 megabytes per second by 50 megabytes per partition requires at least 16 partitions to avoid broker saturation!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Double check the arithmetic! Net growth is 15,000 minus 9,000, which equals 6,000 messages per second. Thirty thousand divided by 6,000 is 5.00 seconds. For Kafka, 800 divided by 50 equals 16 partitions.
